Enhancement of high-solid chicken manure anaerobic digestion: Insights 
into ammonia air stripping pretreatment for microbial resilience and 
hydraulic retention stabilization
Xinhui Yu a, Fangtong Wei b, Haipeng Wang d, Shaojie Bi b,c,*
, Changjiang Zhao a,c,**
,  
Yanjie Wang b,c
a Agricultural College, Heilongjiang Bayi Agricultural University, Daqing, 163319, China

Heilongjiang Bayi Agricultural University, Daqing, 163319, China

Keywords:
Anaerobic digestion
Chicken manure
Microbial community
Pretreatment
Ammonia inhibition
A B S T R A C T
Ammonia inhibition remains a critical barrier in high-solid anaerobic digestion (AD) of nitrogen-rich chicken 
manure. This study demonstrates an ex-situ ammonia air stripping pretreatment system integrated with semi- 
continuous AD, achieving dual objectives of nitrogen mitigation and inorganic solids removal. Through 90- 
day operation at t an organic loading rate (OLR) of 3.1 g-COD/(L⋅d), pretreated chicken manure (PCM) 
exhibited a 20 % higher methane yield (225 vs. 187 mL/g-COD) compared to untreated chicken manure (CM). 
The PCM reactor maintained stable hydraulic retention time (HRT) at 30 days, while the CM reactor suffered a 
20 % effective volume loss. Metagenomic analysis revealed stripping-induced microbial selection favoring 
hydrogenotrophic methanogens (Methanobrevibacter) and syntrophic acetate-oxidizers (Syntrophaceticus), 
enabling stable operation at 5.6 g/L total ammonia nitrogen (TAN) versus the inhibitory threshold (6.4 g/L TAN) 
observed in CM. The pretreatment achieved 28 % total solids (TS) reduction via inorganic solids removal and a 
4.5-fold volatile fatty acids (VFAs) surge (39.9 g-COD/L) through microaeration-enhanced hydrolysis. Spearman 
correlation identified TAN and HRT as dominant determinants of methane yield. This work establishes air 
stripping as a scalable pretreatment strategy, resolving both biological (ammonia inhibition) and engineering 
(HRT instability) bottlenecks in chicken manure valorization and bioenergy production.
1. Introduction
The sustainable valorization of agricultural waste is critical for 
achieving circular bioeconomy objectives. As the world’s largest poultry 
producer, China raised approximately 5.2 billion chickens in 2021, 
generating over 5 million tons of nitrogen-equivalent manure annually 
[1]. This resource contains substantial biodegradable organics (4 %–7 % 
total nitrogen by weight), suitable for energy recovery via anaerobic 
digestion (AD) [2,3]. However, ammonia inhibition constitutes a 
fundamental bottleneck in chicken manure mono-digestion at high total 
solids (TS >10 %). Elevated total ammonia nitrogen (TAN) 
concentrations consistently exceed 4 g/L, resulting in free ammonia 
levels >0.5 g/L. This severely disrupts metabolic pathways, reduces 
methanogenic populations, accumulates volatile fatty acids (VFAs), and 
causes pH disturbances. Ultimately, this cascade drives >30 % methane 
yield reductions, chronic reactor instability, and significant economic 
losses at high organic loading rates (OLR) [4,5], making ammonia in­
hibition mitigation essential for stable high-solids AD operation.
The root challenge lies in ammonia partitioning dynamics. As TS 
increases in high-solid systems, free ammonia concentration rises

[6]. Bi et al. demonstrated that dry AD of chicken manure (20 % TS, OLR 
= 7.1 g-VS/(L⋅d)) led to process failure despite relative ammonia 
tolerance in Methanosarcina and Methanoplasma; whereas wet systems 
(5 % TS, OLR = 1.7 g-VS/(L⋅d)) achieved 280 mL/g-VS methane yield 
[7]. Crucially, whether high-solid AD can function stably at lowered 
OLRs under ammonia stress remains unresolved.
Current mitigation strategies exhibit limitations. Biochemical 
methods (trace element supplementation, Methanoculleus spp. bio­
augmentation) recover only 15 %–20 % methane under moderate TAN 
(<4 g/L) but fail in high-solids systems where ammonia partitioning 
intensifies [8,9]. Co-digestion with high carbon-to-nitrogen (C/N) ratio 
substrates (e.g., crop residues) reduces TAN by ~34 % through nitrogen 
dilution [10], yet feasibility is constrained by geographical scarcity of 
carbon-rich feedstocks near large Chinese biogas plants [11]. Physico­
chemical TAN removal (dilution, vacuum stripping, precipitation) suf­
fers from prohibitive costs and scalability challenges [12,13].
Novel pretreatments show promise for enhancing AD resilience. 
Static magnetic fields (SMF), for instance, modulate microbial commu­
nities: low-intensity SMF (20 mT) increased sewage sludge biomethane 
yield by 12.7 %, while high-intensity SMF (1.5 T) inhibited production 
by 15.1 % [14]. Such targeted interventions underscore pretreatment 
value. Ammonia stripping leverages NH4
+/NH3 phase transitions for ni­
trogen removal. While established in wastewater treatment [15], its 
application to high-solid AD faces critical knowledge gaps including: (1) 
microbial community resilience post-stripping, particularly hydro­
genotrophic methanogens’ capacity to maintain syntrophy with 
acetate-oxidizing bacteria under residual ammonia stress; and (2) 
uncharacterized synergies between ammonia removal and inorganic 
solids reduction (e.g., grit, sand) [16].
Recent advances confirm that TAN reduction through stripping al­
leviates acetoclastic methanogens inhibition [17], while introduced air 
enhances organic solubilization under microaerobic conditions [18]. Bi 
et al. demonstrated that in-situ biogas stripping reduced TAN by 20 % 
during high-solid chicken manure AD (15 % TS) [19]. However, no 
studies have systematically evaluated ex-situ air stripping pretreatment 
for continuous high-solid chicken manure AD (≥10 % TS), leaving im­
pacts on nitrogen removal, methane production, microbial ecology, and 
inorganic solids mitigation uncharacterized.
This study pioneers the integration of ex-situ ammonia stripping 
pretreatment with high-solid chicken manure AD (12 % TS), addressing 
nitrogen removal efficiency and methane production, microbial com­
munity shifts underpinning process stability, and the synergistic effects 
of ammonia stripping and inorganic solids removal on hydraulic reten­
tion time (HRT) preservation. By integrating physicochemical and 
metagenomic analyses, this work provides novel insights into ammonia 
stripping scalability for biogas systems, advancing sustainable valori­
zation strategies for nitrogen-rich agricultural waste.
2. Materials and methods
2.1. Inoculum and substrates
The inoculum was obtained from a laboratory-scale continuously 
stirred tank reactor (CSTR) acclimated to chicken manure digestion for 
over 6 months at 37 ◦C (pH = 7.4). The inoculum had a TS content of 4.9 
% (wet weight). Volatile solids (VS) comprised 53.1 % of the TS. Fresh 
chicken manure (TS = 42.1 %, VS/TS ratio = 69.6 %) was collected from 
a poultry farm in Daqing, China. The manure was diluted to 12 % TS 
with deionized water, and homogenized using a blender (L12-Y3, Joy­
oung, China) to ensure uniformity. The substrate was aliquoted into 500 
mL vials and stored at 4 ◦C throughout the experimental period.
2.2. Experimental set-up and operations
Two parallel 10-L CSTRs were operated at 37 ◦C with a working 
volume of 8 L. Each reactor was equipped with a paddle-type agitator 
(100 rpm), a water jacket, and a heated circulation system for temper­
ature control. Both reactors were fed daily with either pretreated 
chicken manure (PCM) or untreated chicken manure (CM) at an OLR of 
3.1 g-chemical oxygen demand (COD)/(L⋅d) and an HRT of 30 days, 
reflecting industrial-scale biogas plant conditions [11]. Biogas produc­
tion, composition (CH4 and CO2), and pH levels were monitored daily. 
Additionally, the concentrations of COD, TAN, and VFAs in the digestate 
were analyzed every 10 days.
The ammonia stripping system (Fig. 1) was integrated into the PCM 
reactor, operating at 37 ◦C with a 2-day HRT. Key parameters included 
cyclic aeration (15 s every 5 min at 2 L/min flow rate) following prior 
optimization [19]. The stripped ammonia was then absorbed in an 800 
mL scrubber containing 5 M sulfuric acid (H2SO4) for neutralization, 
which facilitated the recovery of ammonium sulfate. The CM reactor 
operated identically without stripping.
2.3. Chemical analysis
The determination of TS and VS was performed using gravimetric 
analysis. Samples were dried at 105 ◦C for a minimum of 24 h and at 
600 ◦C for at least 6 h. The concentrations of total COD, soluble COD, 
and TAN were measured following the methods outlined by the Amer­
ican Public Health Association [20]. VFAs including acetate, propionate, 
butyrate, valerate, and caproate were analyzed according to a previous 
study [21]. pH was measured using a pH meter (PHS-3C; Yidi, Shanghai, 
China). Biogas yield was quantified daily with a wet biogas meter 
(LML-1; Hongke, Shanghai, China) and calibrated to standard conditions 
of temperature (273.15 K) and pressure (1 atm). Biogas composition was 
analyzed using a gas chromatograph (GC-7890; Jinpu, Shandong, 
China) equipped with a 2 m long and 3 mm inner diameter capillary 
column (TDX-01; Jinpu). The column, injector, and detector tempera­
tures were maintained at 100 ◦C, 100 ◦C, and 50 ◦C, respectively, with 
hydrogen serving as the carrier gas.
2.4. Microbial community analysis
Digestate samples (PCM and CM reactors) and substrates were 
collected on day 83 (steady-state) and stored at −80 ◦C until further 
metagenomic analysis. Triplicate samples were sent to Meiji Company 
for DNA extraction, quality testing, sequencing, and sequence analysis. 
Specifically, DNA was extracted using the CTAB/SDS method, followed 
by purification (1 % agarose gel) and quantification (NanoDrop 2000, 
Thermo Fisher). The purified DNA was used for PCR amplification of 
bacterial and archaeal 16S rRNA genes. For bacterial sequences, the 
primers was 338F (5′-ACTCCTACGGGAGGCAGCAG-3′) and 806R (5′- 
GGACTACHVGGG TWTCTAAT-3′) were used, while for archaeal se­
quences, the primers 524F (5′-TGY CAG CCG CCGCGGTAA-3′) and 958R 
(5′-YCCGGCGTTGAVTCCAATT-3′) [22]. The PCR products were puri­
fied, quantified, and sequenced using the Illumina MiSeq platform (2 ×
300 bp paired-end). Raw sequences were quality-filtered (Trimmomatic 
v0.38), denoised (DADA2), and clustered into operational taxonomic 
units (OTUs) at 97 % similarity (UPARSE) [19]. Taxonomic classifica­
tion was performed using the SILVA database (v138), and functional 
annotation utilized FAPROTAX [23]. Most annotated species were 
assigned to groups associated with essential metabolic and ecological 
functions, including C, N, and S biogeochemical cycling and organic 
matter degradation.
2.5. Calculations and statistics
Data are presented as mean ± standard deviation (n = 3). Signifi­
cance between reactors was assessed via Student’s t-test (p < 0.05). All 
analyses were performed in Origin 9.1.
Hydrolysis, acidogenesis, and acetogenesis efficiencies were calcu­
lated using COD mass balance equations (Eqs. (1)–(3)) [24].

3. Results
3.1. Substrate transformation through pretreatment process
Stripping pretreatment significantly altered the physicochemical 
properties of chicken manure (Table 1). TS decreased by 28 % (p <
0.05), indicating efficient inorganic removal (e.g., ash), while total COD 
remained stable (p = 0.766), confirming minimal organic matter loss—a 
critical factor for preserving energy potential. Soluble COD increased by 
51 % (from 36.1 to 54.4 g-COD/L, p < 0.05), reflecting enhanced sol­
ubilization of particulate organics. Additionally, VFAs surged 4.5-fold 
(from 8.9 to 39.9 g-COD/L, p < 0.05), predominantly consisting of ac­
etate (30 %), propionate (18 %), and butyrate (20 %) (Table 1), sug­
gesting that microaeration promotes hydrolysis and acidogenesis, 
consistent with studies on complex wastes [18].
In terms of nitrogen dynamics, total nitrogen decreased by 14 % 
(from 6.65 to 5.72 g/L, p < 0.05), while TAN increased by 108 % (from 
2.4 to 5.0 g/L, p < 0.05) (Table 1). This paradox arises from the dual 
mechanisms of pretreatment: the volatilization of free NH3 and the hy­
drolysis of organic nitrogen (e.g., proteins) into NH4
+, which tends to 
accumulate unless fully stripped.
Conversion efficiencies for hydrolysis (31.9 %), acidogenesis (36.6 
%), and acetogenesis (12.5 %) aligned closely with thermophilic 
anaerobic benchmarks (70 ◦C) [25], demonstrating that microaerobic 
stripping can achieve comparable efficiency at lower mesophilic tem­
peratures (37 ◦C) with reduced energy costs.
3.2. The enhancement of methanogenic performance
Throughout the 87-day fermentation, the PCM reactor maintained 
lower TAN levels (Fig. S1) and achieved higher methane productivity 
than the untreated CM reactor (Fig. 2). Notably, methane yield in the 
PCM reactor remained stable (linear regression slope, k = −0.04), 
whereas the CM reactor exhibited a significant decline (k = −0.45), 
decreasing from 203 to 187 mL/g-COD across three HRT stages (Fig. 2a). 
By the third HRT, the PCM reactor achieved a yield of 225 mL/g-COD 
(64 % of the theoretical maximum of 350 mL/g-COD), outperforming 
the CM reactor by 20 % (p < 0.05, Fig. 2b).
Spearman’s correlation analysis (Fig. 3a) of operational parameters 
(Table 2) revealed methane yield was negatively correlated with TAN, 
OLR, VFA accumulation, and feed concentration (TS and COD), but 
positively correlated with HRT and substrate pretreatment. Under suit­
able conditions (OLR = 3.1 g-COD/(L⋅d), HRT = 30 d), PCM achieved 
225 mL/g-COD with low VFAs (1.9 g/L) and moderate TAN (5.6 g/L). In 
contrast, CM yielded only 187 mL/g-COD despite identical parameters, 
accompanied by higher TAN (6.4 g/L) and VFAs (6.5 g/L). PCM sur­
passed literature benchmarks at similar or lower OLRs [26–28], pri­
marily due to ammonia stripping pretreatment, which reduced TAN by 
12.5 % versus CM (p < 0.05; Table 2).
The pretreatment system also removed sand and stones from the 
manure, ensuring sufficient HRT within the PCM reactor. Industrial 
biogas plants prioritize stable operation under high OLR and low HRT 
for profitability [32]. Unscreened chicken manure requires a minimum 
HRT of 40 days [30] due to 8 %–10 % TS as sand amd stones entrapped

Linear regression was conducted to assess the effects of TAN and HRT 
on methane yield. The analysis confirmed that increased HRT (≥30 
days) enhanced methane yield, with higher HRT values exceeding the 
fitted trendline and lower values falling below predictions (Fig. 3b). 
PCM consistently exceeded regression predictions, while untreated CM 
fell below the trendline, indicating inorganic removal improved 
methane production (Fig. 3c). The CM reactor’s effective volume 
decreased by approximately 20 % during digestion (actual HRT = 24 
days), directly reducing methane output. Conversely, PCM maintained 
stable productionat the target HRT of 30 days.
These results underscore the dual role of ammonia stripping: (1) 
reducing TAN by 12.5 %, alleviating inhibition of acetoclastic metha­
nogens (e.g., Methanosaeta); and (2) removing inorganic solids, pre­
venting HRT shortening via solids accumulation. This highlights the 
stripping efficiency in enabling stable high-rate digestion (HRT = 30 
days) without sacrificing methane output—a critical advantage for in­
dustrial biogas plants prioritizing reactor volume minimization and 
operational continuity [32]. Furthermore, the removal of sand and 
stones not only preserved HRT but also enhanced process economics by 
reducing maintenance costs associated with pump wear and grit 
removal [33].
3.3. The enhancement of methane conversion rate
Comparing the conversion of organic matter into soluble COD, VFAs, 
and methane in PCM and CM reactors (Fig. 4), the CM reactor exhibited 
a higher fraction of particulate COD, indicating a higher proportion of 
non-degraded organic matter (28.9 %) than that in the PCM reactor 
(23.9 %). This result suggested that stripping pretreatment enhanced the 
efficiency of organic matter breakdown in the PCM reactor. In addition, 
the CM reactor exhibited higher levels of soluble COD and VFAs than the 
PCM reactor, likely due to TAN inhibition of methanogenesis, leading to 
VFA accumulation [7,34,35]. The PCM reactor demonstrated that 
methane conversion rate of 65.7 %, which was 23.1 % higher than that 
of CM reactor, highlighting the benefits of stripping pretreatment in 
enhancing hydrolysis, acidogenesis, and methane production.
3.4. Variations of bacterial community
High-throughput sequencing revealed Firmicutes (66.4 %–83.1 %) 
as the dominant bacterial phylum across all samples (Fig. 5a), consistent 
with studies linking its hydrolytic and acidogenic versatility to enhanced 
VFA production under high OLRs conditions [34,36,37]. Substantial 
variations among the sampled specimens were observed at the genus 
level (Fig. 5b). The higher abundance of Lachnospiraceae NK3A20 in 
PCM versus untreated CM aligns with accelerated carbohydrate degra­
dation [38], explaining the 4.5-fold VFA surge during pretreatment 
(Table 1). The PCM reactor was dominated by Fastidiosipila, Gallicola, 
and Lachnospiraceae NK3A20, contrasting sharply with CM reactor’s 
prevalence of Proteiniphilum, MBA03, and Thiopseudomonas in the CM 
reactor. This enrichment of specialized genera (Fastidiosipila, Gallicola) 
capable of converting uric acid and proteins to acetate and butyrate [19,
39] diverges from CM reactor’s nitrogen-tolerant genera (Proteiniphilum, 
Thiopseudomonas) thriving under methanogenic inhibition. Elevated 
VFAs generated substrate pools for syntrophic consortia. Consequently, 
Clostridium and Syntrophaceticus were slightly enriched in PCM (1.1 % 
vs. 0.7 % in CM), potentially aiding methane production [40].
Functional annotation using FAPROTAX identified 43 ecological 
functions, with chemoheterotrophy and fermentation (20 %–50 %) 
being predominant (Fig. 5c). The pathogen-related functions associated 
with animal parasites or symbionts, human gut, mammalian gut, and 
human pathogens were detected only in untreated manure, suggesting 
efficient pathogen removal during stripping pretreatment and AD pro­
cesses. Furthermore, ecological functions related to nitrite respiration, 
reduction, and ammonification were exclusively detected at high levels 
in untreated manure, indicating the presence of nitrogen-metabolizing 
bacteria. These results suggested that the pretreatment process 
reduced the nitrogen content of the substrate.
3.5. Variations of archaeal community
The Archaeal communities in unpretreated CM, PCM and reactors 
were compared at the phylum level. Euryarchaeota dominated archaeal 
communities except in untreated CM, where Crenarchaeota prevailed 
(Fig. 6a). Euryarchaeota includes key AD methanogens. Significant 
genus-level differences existed between the CM and PCM reactors 
(Fig. 6b). Methanobrevibacter was enriched in the PCM reactor, con­
trasting with Methanobacterium and Methanoculleus in the CM reactor. 
Previous studies have shown that methanogens in these genera are 
commonly found in AD processes with high levels of TAN and have 
demonstrated tolerance to ammonia, effectively acting as methanogenic 
partners in syntrophic acetate oxidation [7,41]. Methanobacterium and 
Methanoculleus were both identified in the anaerobic reactors used to 
treat chicken manure, and their dominance was observed in conjunction 
with significant VFA accumulation and low methane production. 
Methanobrevibacter enrichment in PCM reactor, known for ammonia 
tolerance and syntrophic acetate oxidation, likely contributed to supe­
rior methane production [42].
Functional annotation of the archaeal taxa was performed using the 
FAPROTAX database and the archaeal communities were annotated 
with 10 ecological functions, including hydrogenotrophic methano­
genesis (mainly in PCM, CM and PCM reactors) and aerobic ammonia 
oxidation in the untreated CM samples (Fig. 6c).

4. Discussion
4.1. Comparison with other similar studies
This study establishes ex-situ ammonia air stripping as a highly 
effective pretreatment strategy for overcoming ammonia inhibition and 
HRT instability in high-solids AD of chicken manure. By integrating 
stripping with semi-continuous AD (PCM reactor), a significant 20 % 
increase in methane yield (225 vs. 187 mL/g-COD) was achieved while 
maintaining stable HRT of 30 days. This was underpinned by a 28 % 
reduction in TS through inorganic solids removal and a dramatic 4.5- 
fold increase in VFAs (39.9 g-COD/L) facilitated by microaeration- 
enhanced hydrolysis. Metagenomic analysis revealed this performance 
was driven by microbial community restructuring, specifically the se­
lective enrichment of hydrogenotrophic methanogens (Methano­
brevibacter) and syntrophic acetate-oxidizing bacteria (Syntrophaceticus), 
enabling stable methanogenesis at elevated TAN levels (5.6 g/L). Fig. 7
summarizes the proposed process mechanism for enhanced AD 
performance.

research on ammonia stripping for nitrogen-rich wastes. The demon­
strated efficacy in mitigating ammonia toxicity confirms core principles 
established in studies across different feedstocks. For instance, stripping 
of piggery wastewater significantly enhanced methane productivity 
[43], while studies on poultry manure also reported substantial in­
creases in methane yield (e.g., 30–34 % improvements [19,44]) through 
ammonia removal. Our observed shift towards hydrogenotrophic 
methanogenesis, supported by enriched Syntrophaceticus and Methano­
brevibacter, resonates with findings where stripping or similar mitiga­
tions (e.g., biochar addition [45]) enriched hydrogenotrophic pathways 
(Methanoculleus, Methanothermobacter) or syntrophic partners under 
high ammonia stress [46–48]. Furthermore, this study directly addresses 
a critical operational bottleneck often overlooked in fundamental 
research: HRT instability caused by inorganic solids accumulation. The 
removal of grit and sand during stripping proved essential for preventing 
reactor clogging and preserving stable HRT, addressing a key failure 
mode in industrial-scale systems [19,44]. This operational benefit, 
combined with the biological mitigation, represents a holistic engi­
neering solution. While variations exist in methane yield improvements 
reported (ranging from ~20 % to >350 % depending on initial inhibi­
tion severity and mitigation strategy [44,48,49]), the magnitude of our 
increase (20 %) is consistent within the context of successful pretreat­
ment under high-solids conditions and aligns with optimized systems 
like those enhanced by biogas recirculation stripping [13]. The differ­
ences can be attributed to factors such as pretreatment intensity (pH, 
duration, microaeration inclusion), stripping configuration (ex-situ vs. 
in-situ [13,50]), substrate properties, and operating conditions (OLR, 
temperature). Our focus on microaeration-enhanced hydrolysis during 
stripping as a driver for VFA surge adds a novel operational dimension to 
the 
pretreatment 
effect. 
The 
concomitant 
reduction 
in 
pathogen-associated functions adds another valuable benefit consistent 
with improved process sanitation observed in other stripping studies 
[50].
4.2. Research limitations and future perspectives
While this study demonstrates the clear benefits of ex-situ ammonia 
air stripping integrated with AD for high-solids chicken manure man­
agement, contributing significantly to both biological stability and 
operational robustness, several limitations warrant consideration.
As highlighted for future work, the optimization of stripping dura­
tion and gas-liquid contact efficiency was identified as crucial but not 
exhaustively explored here. Maximizing net nitrogen removal while 
minimizing organic carbon loss remains a critical engineering trade-off 
[43]. Findings confirmed the importance of pH control, but potential 
sodium ion inhibition at very high pH values (>10–11), as noted in 
wastewater stripping studies [43,46], requires careful management in 
manure systems where large alkali additions might be needed, sug­
gesting low-cost alkaline agents or pH control strategies are worth 
further investigation.
The integration of ex-situ stripping adds complexity compared to 
single-stage AD or simpler additive strategies (e.g., biochar, allophane 
[45,48,49]). While proven effective here, the economic viability and 
energy balance of this two-stage approach (including the microaeration 
step) at full industrial scale require detailed techno-economic analysis 
and life cycle assessment, building on pilot-scale validations like those 
initiated for related technologies [50].
Although metagenomic analysis revealed key shifts (Methano­
brevibacter, Syntrophaceticus enrichment), the long-term microbial 
community resilience and functional stability under varying substrate 
loads or process disturbances beyond the tested effective volume loss 
scenario need further longitudinal investigation. The integration of 
“microbial resilience metrics with process engineering parameters” 
proposed here provides a framework, but its predictive power needs 
validation across more diverse conditions. The interplay between 
stripping-removed nutrients (beyond just TAN) and microbial function 
was not fully characterized.
The study utilized a specific chicken manure source. The effective­
ness and optimal stripping parameters might vary with manure 
composition (depending on diet, bedding, collection methods), which is 
common to all AD research on animal wastes. Testing robustness across 
a range of manure compositions would strengthen broader applicability 
claims.
5. Conclusions
This study demonstrates that ex-situ ammonia air stripping effec­
tively overcomes ammonia inhibition and HRT instability in high-solids 
chicken manure digestion. The pretreatment enabled robust methano­
genesis by enriching specialized ammonia-tolerant microbial consortia, 
while inorganic solids removal prevented reactor volume loss. Concur­
rent ammonia recovery yielded valuable fertilizer, enhancing process 
sustainability. Although operational parameters warrant further opti­
mization, this integrated strategy resolves critical biological and
